title: Learning the Committor Function using Weighted Ensemble Simulations
claim: An iterative loop alternates simulation, data extraction, learning and adaptive resampling, so learning and sampling improve each other.
layout: 6 panels in a clockwise loop, labeled a–f, with a dashed next-iteration arrow
description: Six lettered panels form a clockwise cycle, with labeled arrows between them. Panels a, b, e and f each show a blue double-well free-energy curve over a committor axis from 0 to 1. Dashed vertical lines mark bins, and circular markers are walkers. Marker fill shows weight: the legend gives 1/4, 1/12 and 1/24. Panel a places initial walkers near the two ends. An arrow labeled Propagate leads to panel b, where orange noisy trajectories spread from the walkers. An Extract arrow leads to panel c, a buffer of boxes holding parent–child pairs joined by dotted lines. A Learn arrow, with the self-consistency equation q(x_t)=E[q(x_{t+τ})|x_t], leads to panel d, a small neural network. A Rebin arrow leads to panel e, where bins are denser near the barrier. A Merge + split arrow leads to panel f. A dashed arrow labeled Next iteration returns to b.
caption: Algorithmic overview of WELP, with a target of two walkers per bin: (a) initialize walkers at boundary states; (b) propagate the dynamics; (c) store parent–child pairs in a buffer; (d) train the neural network using the semigroup loss; (e) adaptively rebin to increase sampling in bottleneck regions; and (f) merge and split walkers to restore two walkers per bin.
abstract: Understanding how complex molecular systems transition between metastable states is a central challenge in computational chemistry and biophysics. A key tool for characterizing these transitions is the committor function: the probability that a trajectory initiated from a given configuration reaches one state before another. Because the committor encodes both the progress and the mechanism of a transition, it is an ideal collective variable (CV). Learning it, however, requires sampling the rare transitions it describes. We address this circular dependency with a ``WE-in-the-loop'' framework that couples committor learning with weighted ensemble (WE), an enhanced sampling method that uses a CV to drive transition dynamics. Our framework alternates between the two: WE simulation generates transition data for training a neural network committor with a self-consistent loss, and the learned committor then serves as an improved CV for subsequent WE simulation. Across a two-channel 2D system, alanine dipeptide, and chignolin, our framework consistently outperforms greedy baselines, highlighting the importance of principled exploration. We also curate a public benchmark of empirically determined committor values for alanine dipeptide. Together, the framework and benchmark provide a new method for studying rare transitions in high-dimensional molecular systems and a standard for evaluating committor learning methods.
